After detaching the tricuspid valve patch, the CTI line was extended to the tricuspid annulus, resulting in complete arrhythmia control.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: The outcome of this case suggests that foetal-onset volume overload from severe tricuspid regurgitation may promote early atrial remodelling and arrhythmogenic substrate formation in TVD. Although CTI ablation after the Starnes procedure may be feasible in a small infant, patch-related anatomic barriers may prevent complete lesion formation. Prior catheter ablation sites may be useful intraoperative landmarks for successful surgical ablation.

articles.title: Non-atrial/non-ventricular functional tricuspid valve regurgitation: a case report

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Functional tricuspid regurgitation (fTR) is usually caused by annular dilation and leaflet tethering secondary to right atrial (RA) or right ventricular (RV) remodelling. Rarely, extrinsic factors may impair annular motion.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: We report a 83-year-old woman with constrictive pericarditis who presented with right-sided heart failure and moderate tricuspid regurgitation. Multimodality imaging revealed a thickened pericardium, preserved RA and RV size, and a non-dilated, saddle-shaped annulus with markedly reduced motion. Following pericardiectomy, tricuspid annular mobility normalized, right-sided pressures decreased, and TR improved from moderate to mild. We introduce the term non-atrial/non-ventricular functional tricuspid regurgitation to describe this rare mechanism of isolated annular dysfunction caused by pericardial tethering.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: This case highlights a novel, distinct, and reversible form of fTR caused by pericardial constraint rather than chamber remodelling. We propose the term non-atrial/non-ventricular fTR to describe this mechanism. Recognizing this entity may guide surgical decision-making and avoid unnecessary tricuspid valve intervention.

articles.title: Preliminary experience with controlled hypothermic storage of donor heart in combined heart transplantation

abstract.text: While studies have demonstrated improved clinical outcomes with the use of controlled hypothermic storage (CHS) devices in isolated heart transplantation, it has not been evaluated in combined heart transplantation. In this small retrospective study (n=17), we evaluate clinical outcomes after combined heart-liver and heart-kidney transplantation in recipients of donor hearts preserved with conventional ice cold storage (ICS, n=10) versus CHS (n=7). The study found severe early graft dysfunction (EGD) occurred more frequently in the ICS cohort when compared to the CHS cohort (70% vs 0%, respectively). In addition, the CHS cohort had shorter median intensive care unit length of stay (7 days compared to 15.5 days, respectively) as well as fewer post-transplant complications, including sepsis (60% in ICS and 28.6% in CHS), pneumonia (40% in ICS and 14.3% in CHS), stroke (30% in ICS and 0% in CHS), and acute kidney injury requiring dialysis (60% in ICS and 28.6% in CHS). These preliminary findings suggest CHS may improve outcomes in combined heart transplantation.

articles.title: Waitlist mortality risk (US-CRS score) distribution among status 1 and 2 adult heart transplant candidates with exceptions

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The US-candidate risk score (US-CRS) predicts waitlist mortality among heart transplant candidates using 7 laboratory, cardiovascular, and cardiac device usage variables on a 50-point scale, with higher scores indicating greater mortality risk. We assessed whether US-CRS accurately assigns mortality risk for exception candidates, and whether the alignment of allocation priority with waitlist mortality risk (US-CRS) differs between candidates with and without exceptions.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We compared the performance of US-CRS in candidates with and without exceptions using receiver operating curves. We compared US-CRS distributions using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test and examined the proportion of candidates below specific score thresholds in each group. We also compared candidates with and without exceptions using Wilcoxon Rank-Sum test for continuous variables and Pearson's Chi-squared test or Fisher exact test for categorical variables.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: US-CRS is accurate for measuring mortality risk among exception candidates as it is among non-exception candidates. Patients with higher waitlist status had higher median US-CRS. However, the median US-CRS of Status 1 candidates without exceptions (50 [IQR 48-50]) was significantly higher than for candidates with exceptions (45 [36-48]; [ p ≤ 0.05 ]), and similarly for Status 2 (46 [41-49] vs. 42 [32-47]; [ p ≤ 0.05 ]). Notably, 33.13% of Status 1 and 41.28% of Status 2 candidates with exceptions had US-CRS below 40, compared to only 1.84% and 19.20% of candidates without exceptions, respectively. Conversely, among candidates in Status 3 and 4, candidates with exceptions generally had higher US-CRS than candidates without exceptions.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Allocation priority under the status system does not align with estimated mortality risk; misalignment is greater for candidates with exceptions. While some exception candidates in Status 1 and 2 do have high estimated mortality risk and legitimately need exceptions, many of these exceptions appear to have been granted to candidates with relatively low medical urgency.

articles.conclusion: Allocation priority under the status system does not align with estimated mortality risk; misalignment is greater for candidates with exceptions. While some exception candidates in Status 1 and 2 do have high estimated mortality risk and legitimately need exceptions, many of these exceptions appear to have been granted to candidates with relatively low medical urgency.

articles.title: Increasing physical activity in pediatric heart transplant recipients: Insights from patients and their families to inform intervention design and implementation

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Survival after pediatric heart transplantation (HT) remains limited, and recipients face a heightened burden of modifiable cardiovascular risk factors. Despite the well-established benefits of physical activity (PA), pediatric HT recipients demonstrate reduced exercise capacity and low participation in moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA). Effective interventions require a nuanced understanding of behavioral determinants influencing PA engagement. This study sought to characterize perceived barriers, facilitators, and intervention preferences among pediatric HT recipients and their caregivers using the Capability-Opportunity-Motivation Behavior (COM-B) framework.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted semi-structured interviews with pediatric HT recipients aged 6-22 years and their caregivers at a single tertiary transplant center. Participants were purposively sampled to ensure variation in age at transplant, diagnosis, time since transplant, and prior exposure to PA interventions. Interviews explored current activity patterns, perceived barriers and facilitators, and preferences for structured exercise programs. Transcripts were analyzed using an integrated thematic approach combining a priori COM-B constructs with inductively derived themes.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Thirty-four interviews were completed with 17 caregiver-patient dyads and one independent adult participant. Participants generally viewed PA as safe, enjoyable, and emotionally beneficial, reflecting strong intrinsic motivation and preserved psychological capability. Social influences-including peers, family members, and opportunities to connect with other transplant recipients-emerged as powerful motivators for sustained engagement. In contrast, logistical factors such as transportation, scheduling conflicts, and distance from the transplant center were the most frequently cited barriers, highlighting limitations in physical opportunity rather than medical constraints. Caregivers emphasized the importance of professional oversight to enhance confidence, while patients and caregivers identified goal setting and progress tracking as key motivational supports. Many participants favored home-based or virtually delivered interventions to improve accessibility.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Pediatric HT recipients appear both willing and capable of participating in physical activity; however, sustained engagement is largely determined by opportunity and social motivation rather than physiologic limitations. Interventions that prioritize accessibility, incorporate peer connection, and provide structured feedback may promote durable behavior change. These findings offer a theory-informed foundation for designing scalable PA interventions aimed at improving long-term cardiovascular health in pediatric HT recipients.

articles.conclusion: Pediatric HT recipients appear both willing and capable of participating in physical activity; however, sustained engagement is largely determined by opportunity and social motivation rather than physiologic limitations. Interventions that prioritize accessibility, incorporate peer connection, and provide structured feedback may promote durable behavior change. These findings offer a theory-informed foundation for designing scalable PA interventions aimed at improving long-term cardiovascular health in pediatric HT recipients.

articles.title: Ventricular tachycardia ablation in late-onset phenotype Fabry disease: a case report

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder that can cause progressive cardiomyopathy, myocardial fibrosis, conduction disease, and malignant ventricular arrhythmias. Ventricular tachycardia (VT) ablation in advanced Fabry cardiomyopathy is challenging, particularly in patients with extensive scar and left ventricular assist device (LVAD) support.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A 71-year-old man with late-onset Fabry disease, confirmed by endomyocardial biopsy showing myelin body accumulation, reduced α-galactosidase A activity, and elevated plasma Gb3, developed severe left ventricular dysfunction, extensive late gadolinium enhancement, LVAD implantation, and complete atrioventricular block requiring dual-chamber pacemaker implantation. He presented with recurrent palpitations and near-syncope. Device interrogation revealed multiple VT episodes, including one episode degenerating into ventricular fibrillation, and surface electrocardiography documented wide-complex tachycardia with right bundle branch block morphology and an inferior axis. An electrophysiological study was performed using an antegrade transseptal left ventricular approach. Intracardiac echocardiography was used to delineate the LV cavity and LVAD position, facilitating safe catheter navigation and mapping while avoiding interference with the LVAD. Endocardial mapping demonstrated diffuse late potentials, low-voltage substrate, and deceleration zones involving the basal-to-mid-inferolateral left ventricle. Substrate modification targeting these abnormal electrograms eliminated inducible ventricular premature complexes. No recurrent VT episodes were detected on subsequent pacemaker interrogation.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: This case highlights the complex arrhythmogenic substrate of late-stage Fabry cardiomyopathy and the utility of intracardiac echocardiography-guided mapping in patients with LVAD support. Catheter ablation may provide short-term arrhythmia control, but in advanced Fabry disease, its role remains largely palliative.

articles.title: Sex-specific association between body mass index and mortality after heart transplantation: A nationwide KOTRY Cohort Study

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Body mass index has paradoxical associations with outcomes in advanced heart failure, but whether its relationship with survival after heart transplantation differs by sex remains uncertain.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We analyzed 1059 adult heart transplant recipients enrolled in the Korean Organ Transplantation Registry from 2014 through 2023. Body mass index was assessed using Asian-specific BMI categories and 3-knot restricted cubic splines. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Multivariable Cox models adjusted for prespecified clinical characteristics and pretransplant support. Sex differences in the body mass index-mortality association were evaluated using restricted cubic spline modeling.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The cohort included 304 female patients, and 217 deaths occurred during a median follow-up of 3.6 years. The body mass index-mortality association differed by sex in the pooled spline model (P for interaction=0.041). In male patients, the association was nonlinear and U-shaped (P for overall association=0.031; P for nonlinearity=0.017). Underweight was associated with higher mortality than normal weight (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.97; 95% confidence interval, 1.17-3.33). In female patients, the fitted association was inverse, without evidence of nonlinearity (P for overall association=0.030; P for nonlinearity=0.302). Obesity class I was associated with lower mortality than normal weight (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.24; 95% confidence interval, 0.08-0.73), although this estimate was based on few events.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: The association between body mass index and mortality after heart transplantation may differ by sex. The apparent lower mortality among female patients with obesity class I is hypothesis-generating and requires external validation.

articles.conclusion: The association between body mass index and mortality after heart transplantation may differ by sex. The apparent lower mortality among female patients with obesity class I is hypothesis-generating and requires external validation.
